items.title: CVE-2026-84691 - Automation-controller: automation-controller-container: automation-controller: format string injection in the api 4xx error log setting discloses django secret_key and database credentials to an administrator
items.one_liner: A format string vulnerability in Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform allows administrators to extract Django secrets and database passwords via crafted 4XX error logs.
items.summary: A format string injection vulnerability exists in Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform's automation-controller within the API 4XX error log setting (CVE-2026-84691). Because Python string formatting allows attribute traversal on its arguments, an authenticated administrator can craft a template that walks from a live user object into application settings, exposing the Django secret key and database password. If logs are forwarded to an administrator-controlled aggregator, the master encryption key and database password can be exfiltrated for offline decryption of credentials.
key_facts: CVE-2026-84691: Format string injection in automation-controller API 4xx error log setting
Impact: Discloses Django secret_key and database credentials
items.bottom_line: CVE-2026-84691 allows admins to extract Django secrets and database passwords via format string injection in Ansible automation-controller logs.

items.title: From Inference Engine to Inference Control Plane: Connecting vLLM, llm-d, and the Evolution of Efficient Distributed LLM Serving
items.one_liner: LLM serving is shifting from engine-local optimizations to a distributed inference control plane managing state, placement, and network movement.
items.summary: Large language model inference is transitioning from local engine optimizations into a distributed control problem handling state, phase placement, hardware heterogeneity, networking, and service-level objectives across a fleet. This paper examines vLLM and llm-d as complementary layers, where serving engines optimize local execution via PagedAttention and continuous batching, while an inference control plane manages routing, placement, and reliability policies. The authors propose an Inference Execution Planner to select feasible execution topologies, disaggregated KV caching configurations, and routing policies. The findings suggest that scarce resources in modern inference are shifting from raw FLOPs alone toward managed state, network movement, and decision quality.
items.bottom_line: Modern LLM inference requires shifting focus from raw FLOPs to a distributed inference control plane that coordinates managed state, caching topologies, and cluster-wide execution policies.

items.title: AgentBetta: Verification-Driven Adaptive Configuration of an AI Nano-Agent through Selective Expansion and Verified Contraction
items.one_liner: AgentBetta dynamically adjusts LLM agent configurations and tool exposure based on verification, cutting context usage while maintaining task success.
items.summary: Researchers introduce AgentBetta, an adaptive AI nano-agent framework that represents execution factors—such as model capabilities, context window, tools, permissions, and memory—as an executable configuration updated via verification-driven diagnosis, selective expansion, and counterfactual contraction. On the AB-ConfigBench benchmark, AgentBetta achieved 91.38% verified success while reducing median context allocation from 64,000 to 8,000 characters and median tool exposure from five tools to zero compared to fully provisioned configurations. Configuration-deficiency diagnosis achieved a macro-F1 score of 0.819 with perfect precision. However, cross-family replications showed that adaptive configuration performance varies, meaning it serves as an effective capability-regulation mechanism rather than a universal replacement for specialized architectures.
items.bottom_line: AgentBetta demonstrates that verification-driven dynamic configuration can significantly reduce tool exposure and context overhead for LLM agents without sacrificing task success rates.

items.title: Replication Without Persistence in Hosted LLMs: Measurement Sensitivity in Action-Time Belief Evaluation
items.one_liner: Accounting for measurement sensitivity and configuration changes is critical when evaluating hosted LLM performance across different serving periods.
items.summary: Researchers analyzed measurement sensitivity and behavioral persistence in hosted large language models using Regent Chess, an environment featuring an observable, mutable state. The study separated historical replication, measurement sensitivity (endpoint shifts when configurations are rebuilt under identical identifiers), and persistence across distinct model identifiers. Results demonstrated that a previously observed Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite performance deficit recurred on fresh data, but rebuilding configurations altered endpoints, and comparisons between Gemini 3.1 and 3.7 reversed behavioral signs. The findings indicate that hosted-model evaluations are highly sensitive to configuration and serving-period fluctuations.
items.bottom_line: Hosted LLM behavioral evaluations vary significantly due to measurement sensitivity, showing that rebuilding configurations or changing model identifiers can alter or reverse benchmark findings.

items.title: Do Not Trust the Benchmark: Limitations of General LLM Rankings and a Case for Task-Specific Evaluation
items.one_liner: General LLM leaderboards fail to reflect real-world utility, making task-specific evaluation essential for practical model selection.
items.summary: This perspective article on arXiv examines five fundamental limitations of general large language model rankings, arguing that overall scores are tightly coupled to specific tested systems and questions. The author discusses how commercial incentives, benchmark saturation, data contamination, and model manipulation obscure actual performance. To address these issues, the paper advocates for task-specific evaluation procedures that disclose tested configurations, report metrics alongside cost and execution time, and rely on crowd-sourced platforms like Isotanta for repeated task evaluation. Ultimately, the analysis concludes that practical model selection requires evidence of performance on specific intended work rather than reliance on leaderboards.
items.bottom_line: Relying on general LLM leaderboards is fundamentally flawed due to data contamination and commercial biases; task-specific performance data is required for proper model selection.

items.title: TicTacBench: Benchmarking Timing Closure Capabilities of Coding Agents
items.one_liner: TicTacBench evaluates coding agents on RTL timing closure, showing that frontier LLMs struggle with post-PnR optimization unless guided by specialized procedures.
items.summary: Researchers introduce TicTacBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate coding agents on register-transfer level (RTL) timing closure under post-place-and-route (post-PnR) evaluation. The benchmark contains 30 diverse tasks featuring suboptimal RTL designs, timing constraints, and verification reports. Across 300 runs driven by eight frontier LLMs, the best agent successfully closed only 53.3% of tasks, with an average 7.18% area-delay product (ADP) degradation and an 8.83% energy-delay-squared product (EDDP) improvement. The authors also propose TicTacSkill, a method guiding agents through standard timing-closure procedures that improves the timing closure rate by 9%.
items.bottom_line: TicTacBench reveals that even frontier LLMs struggle with RTL timing closure, successfully closing only 53.3% of tasks until guided by specialized procedural methods like TicTacSkill.

items.title: A2M: Trace-Optimized Agent Hijacking in the MCP Ecosystem
items.one_liner: A2M exploits Model Context Protocol semantic matching to hijack AI agents via malicious tool metadata and execution traces.
items.summary: A2M (Attraction-to-Manipulation) is a two-stage black-box framework that exploits semantic matching in Model Context Protocol (MCP) ecosystems to hijack agent behavior. The Attraction phase optimizes third-party tool metadata to increase invocation probability, while the Manipulation phase uses execution traces to refine adversarial tool returns. Tested on LiveMCPBench using GLM-4.6, direct attacks achieved a macro-average malicious tool invocation rate of 93.6%, increased weighted token costs by 32.4 times under Cognitive Denial of Service, and attained a mean attack success rate of 74.4% across multiple exploitation scenarios. Cross-model transfer without re-optimization yielded a 63.6% invocation rate, highlighting severe supply-chain risks in tool-augmented agent architectures.
items.bottom_line: Model Context Protocol ecosystems face critical supply-chain risks where manipulated tool metadata can hijack agent execution flows.

items.title: Formally Modeling the Terrapin Attack on SSH
items.one_liner: A new formal model for SSH channel integrity shows that multiple AEAD modes are insecure against ciphertext-only attacks.
items.summary: Researchers proposed a formal model for channel integrity under partially chosen states to analyze the Terrapin attack on SSH, addressing gaps in existing stateful encryption models. By evaluating pseudocode descriptions across eight prominent AEAD modes and varying the SND oracle, the authors established concrete security bounds for ciphertext-only, known-plaintext, and chosen-plaintext attacks. The analysis reveals that all three Encrypt-then-MAC modes and ChaCha20-Poly1305 in SSH are insecure in the ciphertext-only model, leaving AES-GCM as the only cipher secure across all three variants. Additionally, the work uncovered a novel BEAST-like chosen-plaintext attack on Encrypt-and-MAC with CBC ciphers.

Insecure in CO model: EtM modes and ChaCha20-Poly1305
